senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀγανάκτησις ‘indignation,’ 88.186) to be indignant against what is judged to be wrong

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to not being prejudiced

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act in defiance of social and moral standards, with resulting disgrace, embarrassment, and shame
senses.comment: Behavior involving disgrace, embarrassment, and shame is often expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bury one’s face,’ ‘to hide one’s eyes,’ or ‘to feel stabbed by people’s eyes.’ Since shame is seemingly a universal type of feeling, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: male domestic fowl, dark brownish red, with orange-red neck hackles, a smallish red comb on the top of the head, and red lappets on each side under the beak; the hen is a lighter brownish red and has a smaller comb; significance in the Bible seems related to the fact that cocks crow very early in the morning, announcing the coming dawn
strong affirmation of what is declared
to cause something to become new and different, with the implication of becoming superior
to cause a change to a previous, preferable state
one who sells persons as slaves, including one who kidnaps persons and sells them
to respond to a question, with emphasis upon an implied opposition or contradiction
to express disapproval in return
the first portion of something which has been set aside and offered to God before the rest of the substance or objects can be used
the first of a set, often in relation to something being given
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπαρχή[a] ‘first portion,’ 53.23) a foretaste and pledge of blessings to come
senses.comment: In many respects ἀπαρχή[c] parallels closely the meaning of ἀρραβών (57.170).

senses.def: that which one looks forward to with eagerness and desire
senses.comment: In Romans 8:19 (see 25.63) ἀποκαραδοκία serves in some respects to reinforce the meaning of ἀπεκδέχομαι, but it appears to add a significant component of desire.

senses.def: to speak, with focus upon verbal sound rather than upon content
to be sick or ill, as a state of powerlessness
pertaining to a lack of love or affection for close associates or family

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: humility associated with simplicity of life
the ‘family name’ of the apostle Simon Peter

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
senses.def: a document consisting of a scroll or book
senses.comment: The books referred to in Acts 19:19 consisted of sheets of parchment or of papyrus sewn together in the form of long scrolls or bound in the form of a book.

senses.def: the contents of a book
relatively short statements in written form

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: high quality cloth made from the stems of the flax plant; known for its strength and coolness
a new, sweet wine in process of fermentation
a king of Israel and an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move from one side to another of some geographical object (for example, body of water, chasm, valley, etc.)
to pull or tear an object apart

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to contradictory behavior based upon pretense or hypocrisy
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of δίλογος is ‘to speak in two directions’ or ‘to cover one’s thoughts by means of one’s words.’

senses.def: the ability to perform a particular activity or to undergo some experience
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘ability’ in 2 Corinthians 1:8 may be expressed simply by a modal such as ‘can,’ for example, ‘far beyond what we can endure.’

senses.def: the potentiality to exert force in performing some function
a deed manifesting great power, with the implication of some supernatural force
one who has the power to rule
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret δύναμις in Romans 8:38 as meaning a supernatural power (see 12.44).

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of Ephesians 1:21 some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.def: the meaning or significance of a word or statement
senses.comment: It is, of course, also possible to translate 1 Corinthians 14:11 as ‘if I cannot understand what has been said.’

senses.def: to be in a state of pregnancy
senses.comment: This expression contrasts with the meaning of συλλαμβάνω[b] 23.49 in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.

senses.def: to throw out of an area or object

senses.subdomain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ἐκπτύω ‘to spit out,’ not occurring in the NT) to reject, with the implication of a measure of disdain
senses.comment: In a number of languages ‘to reject’ is expressed idiomatically as ‘to throw away,’ ‘to push away,’ or ‘to turn one’s back toward.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: a person who participates in Greek culture and in so doing would speak the Greek language, but not necessarily a person of Greek ethnic background
senses.comment: In Romans 1:14 it is possible that the contrast Ἕλλησίν τε καὶ βαρβάροις may be interpreted as ‘to the Greek-speaking persons and to those who do not speak Greek,’ but the entire context of Romans 1:14 points to a somewhat broader designation.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an extended meaning of Ἕλλην[a] ‘Greek,’ 11.90) a person who is a Gentile in view of being a Greek
senses.comment: Though the occurrence of Ἕλλην in John 7:35 could be interpreted as merely a reference to Greeks, it is probably a reference to Greeks as being Gentiles, and therefore Ἕλλην[b] is classified here in the subdomain of socio-religious groups. The occurrence of Ἕλλην in Acts 14:1 (ὥστε πιστεῦσαι Ἰουδαίων τε καὶ Ἑλλήνων πολὺ πλῆθος ‘so that a large number of Jews and Gentiles believed’) is another instance of Ἕλλην referring primarily to a socio-religious group rather than merely to Greeks as a nation.

senses.def: to be in a place where one rightfully or normally belongs
(an idiom, literally: to be at home in the body) to be alive, with special emphasis upon physical existence on earth
senses.comment: Most languages have rather generic expressions for ‘life’ or ‘to live,’ but sometimes there are idiomatic expressions which may readily fit the types of contexts illustrated by 2 Corinthians 5:6 and 2 Peter 1:13, for example, ‘to have strength,’ ‘to have one’s eyes,’ and ‘to walk about on the earth.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause a state to be
to dwell more or less permanently in a place which is not one’s own country; (compare related meanings in 11.7.)
a state of prolonged concern and anxiety
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἐπίστασις in 2 Corinthians 11:28, see 35.42.

senses.def: rising up in open defiance of authority, with the presumed intention to overthrow it or to act in complete opposition to its demands
senses.comment: It is also possible that ἀποστασία differs slightly in meaning from ἐπίστασις[b] by virtue of the differences in prefixal formation, but there is insufficient contextual evidence to support such a view.

senses.def: responsibility for oversight based upon authority
senses.comment: Though one might regard ἐπίστασις as meaning only the position of authority, nevertheless this authority is expressed in terms of the oversight and care of others. In a sense the meaning of ἐπίστασις in 2 Corinthians 11:28 is defined by the following appositional phrase, ἡ μέριμνα πασῶν τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν ‘concern for all the churches.’ For another interpretation of ἐπίστασις in 2 Corinthians 11:28, see 25.239.

senses.def: (the diminutive of ἔριφος but without special diminutive meaning) kid, he-goat in the singular and goats in the plural (in the plural form both male and female goats are included in the reference)
senses.comment: Since goats are so widely distributed throughout the world, there is usually little or no difficulty involved in finding a satisfactory term. The difficulty arises, however, in the connotations of the term for goat, especially in contrast with sheep. In contrast with usage in the Bible, in many parts of the tropical world goats are much more highly prized than sheep, because they can forage well for themselves and are appreciated for their meat. Sheep, on the other hand, are often regarded as scavengers and are much less valued. One should not reverse biblical statements about sheep and goats, but marginal notes and a fuller explanation of cultural differences in a glossary are important.

senses.def: a city of uncertain location
causing someone to recover health, often with the implication of having taken care of such a person
the group of servants working in a particular household
the patriarch Jacob, a son of Isaac
the father of Ἰωσήφ[b] in the genealogy of Jesus
the system of Jewish beliefs and customs
senses.comment: In Galatians 1:14 Ἰουδαϊσμός may often be rendered as ‘Jewish religion’ or ‘the way in which Jews believe and behave’ or ‘the ways in which Jews think and do.’

senses.def: pertaining to not being dirty
pertaining to being ritually clean or pure
senses.comment: In Luke 11:41 καθαρός may be rendered in some languages as ‘pure in the eyes of God’ or even ‘right in the eyes of God.’|In a number of languages there is simply no relationship between physical cleanness and ritual acceptability or purity. Accordingly, it may be necessary to render καθαρός in Luke 11:41 and similar contexts as ‘acceptable to God’ or ‘good in God’s eyes’ or ‘good as God thinks.’

senses.def: (a Semitic idiom, literally: the knee bends, or: the knee bows) to bend or bow the knee as a symbol of religious devotion
to speak against, often involving speaking evil of
to flee from an area, with probably greater intensity than in the case of φεύγω[a] and φυγή (15.61)
to become safe by taking refuge
(derivative of κεράμιον ‘earthenware vessel,’ 6.128) one who makes earthenware vessels
a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
senses.comment: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to being modest in the sense of moderate and wellordered
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in 1 Timothy 2:9, see 66.10.

senses.def: pertaining to being proper or suitable in terms of being attractive
senses.comment: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in 1 Timothy 2:9, see 88.48.

senses.def: a percussion instrument consisting of two metal discs which were struck together in order to make a shrill, clashing sound
senses.comment: The equivalent of κύμβαλον is in many instances a phrase such as ‘loud metal.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: a thin layer or peel, especially of skin
senses.comment: In rendering Acts 9:18 it is possible to say ‘there fell from his eyes something which looked like a fish scale’ or ‘… a small flake of skin.’

senses.def: a state of unhappiness marked by regret as a result of what has been done
a state of mental pain and anxiety
to divide into separate parts
to distribute objects to a series of persons
glosses: to give to each in turn

senses.def: to give to someone a part of something

senses.subdomain: Assign to a Role or Function
senses.def: to assign a particular part or aspect of a function or responsibility
glosses: to give a particular task to
to appoint a particular part to

senses.def: the measurement of length
to make an idol in the form of a calf
glosses: to shape an idol in the form of a calf
senses.comment: In order not to appear to contradict the corresponding OT passage (), one may wish to translate this clause in Acts 7:41 as ‘they made an idol in the form of a bull calf.’

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: pertaining to the period of time when one is an adolescent

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the back part of the body from the neck to the pelvis
senses.comment: The phrase τὸν νῶτον … συγκάμπτειν may be regarded as an idiom, since its meaning may be to suffer oppression and trouble. An equivalent expression for ‘and bend their backs forever’ (Romans 11:10) may be ‘to make them slaves forever’ or ‘to make them toil hard forever’ (see 24.94).

senses.def: a state of utter ruin or destruction
to cause the complete destruction or ruin of someone or something
to be seen by or to be visible to, in the sense of being within the range of sight

senses.subdomain: Markers for an Affirmative Response to Questions
senses.def: a marker of a somewhat more emphatic affirmative response
a complete set of instruments used in defensive or offensive warfare (usually, however, with emphasis upon defensive armament, including helmet, shield, breastplate)
senses.comment: πανοπλία is also used figuratively in the NT as a reference to the virtues of Christian character used in the strife against evil: ἐνδύσασθε τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ θεοῦ πρὸς τὸ δύνασθαι ὑμᾶς στῆναι πρὸς τὰς μεθοδείας τοῦ διαβόλου ‘put on all the armor that God gives you, so that you will stand up against the Devil’s evil tricks’ Ephesians 6:11.|Since certain ancient types of armor are no longer used to any extent in fighting, it may be necessary to employ descriptive expressions in order to make clear the types of weapons and/or instruments which were involved. Offensive weapons are often spoken of as ‘tools with which one kills or harms an enemy,’ while defensive armor may be described as ‘what one wears to defend oneself when fighting.’ The complete sense of πανοπλία may then be described in some languages as ‘tools with which one fights against the enemy and what one uses to defend oneself’ or ‘… to protect oneself.’

senses.subdomain: Pass, Cross Over, Go Through, Go Around
senses.def: to move past a reference point
to step on something
senses.comment: It is possible to interpret πατέω in Luke 10:19 as meaning ‘to trample,’ with emphasis upon the impact of the feet upon the snakes (see 19.51). It is important in rendering Luke 10:19 not to give the impression that someone is to merely walk on a mass of snakes; this is simply a matter of accidentally stepping on a poisonous snake or scorpion.

senses.def: to step down on, with the possible implication of continuous or repeated action
senses.comment: The occurrence of πατέω in the figurative context of Revelation 19:15 is based upon the practice of persons squeezing out the juice from grapes by trampling on the grapes in a large vat or container which had an opening at the bottom through which the grape juice could flow.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πατέω[b] ‘to trample,’ 19.51) to harm severely by subjugation
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πατέω in Luke 21:24, see 39.54.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πατέω[b] ‘to trample,’ 19.51) to conquer and keep under subjection
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πατέω in Luke 21:24, see 20.22.

senses.def: a marker of designations of content
senses.comment: This word is found as a variant reading only: γράψαντες ἐπιστολὴν διὰ χειρὸς αὐτῶν περιέχουσαν τάδε ‘writing a letter through them having these (words)’ Acts 15:23 (apparatus).

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of περιέχω ‘to surround,’ not occurring in the NT) to experience an emotion or mood in an overwhelming manner
plausible, but false, speech resulting from the use of well-constructed, probable arguments
(derivative of πνεῦμα[a] ‘Spirit,’ 12.18) one who has received God’s Spirit and presumably lives in accordance with this relationship
glosses: one who has received the Spirit
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to speak of ‘possessing the Spirit,’ but one can often say ‘to be possessed by the Spirit’ or ‘those whom the Spirit possesses’ or ‘… owns’ or ‘… controls.’

senses.def: (derivative of πνεῦμα[a] ‘Spirit,’ 12.18) pertaining to being derived from or being about the Spirit, in reference to such matters as gifts, benefits, teachings, blessings, and religious songs
glosses: from the Spirit (in reference to such matters as gifts, benefits, teachings, blessings, and religious songs)
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 2:13 πνευματικά may perhaps be best rendered in some languages as ‘truths revealed by the Spirit’ or possibly ‘truths about the Spirit.’ Some persons would insist, however, that in 1 Corinthians 2:13 πνευματικά refers to teachings which are of particular benefit or relevance to peoples spirits.|The occurrence of πνευματικός in Ephesians 1:3 and Romans 1:11 could be understood as referring to the human spirit, but the contexts would seem to to point more clearly to the involvement of the Spirit of God. See 26.10.|It is also possible that in Ephesians 5:19 πνευματικαῖς means merely ‘spiritual,’ and as such pertains to what is ‘sacred’ or ‘religious.’ One can, therefore, translate ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς as ‘songs used in worship’ or ‘songs used in worship of God.’ For a discussion of certain related problems involving the rendering of πνευματικός, see 26.10.

senses.def: pertaining to the spiritual nature or being of a person
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret πνευματικός in Ephesians 1:3 as referring to ‘the Holy Spirit,’ that is to say, these blessings would be those which come from the Spirit of God (see 12.21).|In Romans 15:27 (εἰ γὰρ τοῖς πνευματικοῖς αὐτῶν ἐκοινώνησαν τὰ ἔθνη, ὀφείλουσιν καὶ ἐν τοῖς σαρκικοῖς λειτουργῆσαι αὐτοῖς), πνευματικός stands in contrast to σαρκικός[b] ‘material’ (79.1) and may therefore focus upon non-material or spiritual aspects of human personality or life in contrast with the physical aspects. Accordingly, one may translate Romans 15:27 as ‘if the Gentiles shared in their spiritual benefits, they ought to help them with material things.’ It is also possible, however, to understand πνευματικός in Romans 15:27 as referring to those blessings which come from the Holy Spirit (see 12.21) rather than those blessings which are for the human spirit. The terms πνευματικός, ψυχικός, σαρκικός, and σάρκινος reflect considerable overlapping in meaning; see also 26.8 and 79.1-79.6.

senses.def: (derivative of πνεῦμα[a] ‘Spirit of God,’ 12.18) pertaining to a pattern of life controlled or directed by God’s Spirit
pertaining to not being physical
senses.comment: In some languages the concept of ‘spiritual body’ can only be expressed negatively as ‘the body will not have flesh and bones’ or ‘the body will not be a regular body.’

senses.def: pertaining to being supernatural and having its ultimate source in God
senses.comment: In a number of languages this meaning of πνευματικός can only be reflected by a phrase such as ‘which comes from God’ or ‘provided by God.’

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.def: interrogative references to class or kind

senses.subdomain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan
senses.def: (derivative of προτίθεμαι[a] ‘to plan in advance,’ 30.62) that which is planned or purposed in advance
(an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
senses.comment: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

senses.def: an object, usually soft, on which one may lay one’s head
senses.comment: In rendering Mark 4:38 it is important to avoid a translation which would suggest that Jesus was so small or coiled up as to be able to sleep on a single pillow.

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: to be in the first position, with the implication of high rank and prominence

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: a piece of cloth sewed on clothing to repair a hole or tear
a musical wind instrument; made of metal; frequently used in signaling, especially in connection with war
senses.comment: The present-day equivalent of the σάλπιγξ is the bugle.

senses.def: (derivative of σαλπίζω[a] ‘to play the trumpet,’ 6.90) the sound made by a trumpet
senses.comment: With both σαλπίζω[b] (6.92) and σάλπιγξ[b], it may be necessary to introduce an agent, even though indefinite. For example, ἐν τῇ ἐσχάτω σάλπιγγι may be translated as ‘when someone blows the trumpet for the last time,’ and σαλπίσει may be rendered as ‘when someone sounds the trumpet’ or ‘when someone produces a noise on the trumpet.’ However, any term for ‘noise’ should imply a meaningful sound.

senses.def: iron
senses.comment: Since at the present time iron in some form is almost universal throughout the world, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for it. In some instances, in fact, it is such a dominant metal that it is known simply as ‘the metal.’

senses.def: small, soft, legless, tube-shaped creatures that have no bones or shells. They typically feed on overripe fruit, rotting meat, and similar things; most are larvae that hatch from the eggs laid by flies or some beetles; symbols of uncleanness, decay, and death
senses.comment: In Mark 9:48 the reference is clearly to the type of maggots which feed on refuse.|In a number of languages a very important distinction is made between three different types of worms: (1) maggots, (2) worms that live in the ground, so-called ‘earthworms,’ and (3) intestinal worms. It is essential that an appropriate term be employed in order to avoid meaninglessness or misunderstanding.

senses.def: a set of difficult circumstances, implying certain restrictions
senses.comment: ‘Distress’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘people will be in trouble’ or in an idiomatic expression, ‘the world will fall on people.’

senses.def: one who participates with another in some enterprise or matter of joint concern
one who shares jointly with someone else in a possession or relationship, with emphasis upon that which is in common
pertaining to being closely associated in a similar experience
to employ one’s capacity for understanding and thus to arrive at insight
to be able to understand and evaluate

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: the physical body of persons, animals, or plants, either dead or alive
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction must be made between the body of a living person and a dead body (or corpse). Other languages distinguish between the bodies of persons and the bodies of animals, and frequently the term for a body of a plant is distinct from those referring to persons or animals. Often a term for body consists of a phrase, for example, ‘flesh and bones,’ and in a number of languages a reference to the body is made primarily by referring to the person himself. For example, in Matthew 26:12 (‘has poured this ointment on my body’) the appropriate equivalent may be ‘has poured this ointment on me.’ In certain instances ‘body’ may be rendered as something which is experienced. For example, in 1 Corinthians 6:20 ‘glorify God through your body’ may be rendered as ‘glorify God through what you do’ or ‘… do in your body.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σῶμα[a] ‘body,’ 8.1) a person as a physical being, including natural desires

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of σῶμα[a] ‘body,’ 8.1) believers in Christ who are joined together as a group, with the implication of each having a distinctive function within the group
senses.comment: Though in some languages it may seem relatively strange to speak of an organization of persons as a ‘body,’ it is important to try to preserve in one way or another this figurative meaning of σῶμα, since it plays such an important role in various phases of Paul’s teaching. It is frequently necessary, however, to change the metaphor into a simile, as has already been suggested in the translation of Ephesians 4:12.

senses.def: a slave as property to be sold, with the probable implicaton of commerce
an entity which corresponds to an archetype or foreshadowing
(an idiom, literally: heavenly body, occurring in the NT only in the plural) the luminous objects in the sky: sun, moon, and other planets and stars
senses.comment: See also 1.8.|The phrase σῶμα ἐπουράνιον is a highly generic expression which in the plural is sometimes translatable as ‘lights in the sky,’ but more often than not it may be necessary to identify the various heavenly bodies as ‘sun, moon, and stars.’ In certain contexts one may also wish to identify the planets, often spoken of as ‘wandering stars’ or ‘moving stars’ (reflecting the etymology of the English word planet, which is derived from a Greek word meaning ‘wanderer’). These are, of course, not to be confused with shooting stars and comets in the sky.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to leave home from the body) euphemistic expressions for dying
to produce completely mature fruit

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
senses.def: topaz, usually yellow in color (see 2.29)
the process of burning slowly, with accompanying smoke and relatively little glow
senses.comment: In Matthew 12:20 the burning of the wick may be described as ‘to burn very slowly’ or ‘to burn just a little,’ but it may be more satisfactory to render τύφομαι in terms of the amount of light which is shown, for example, ‘causing just a little light’ or ‘shining only a little as it burns.’

senses.def: to experience something to which a person is subjected
to shine or to produce light, as in the case of heavenly bodies, lightning, candles, torches, etc.
senses.comment: Terms for ‘shining, giving light’ often differ depending upon the type of source. There may be, for example, a contrast between the shining of a heavenly body in contrast with some source on earth. There may also be a difference between a continuous shining such as of the sun and the moon and a brief flash, as in the case of lightning or sparks from a fire.

senses.def: to become visible to someone
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘appeared to’ would simply be ‘came to’ or ‘arrived at.’ In other languages the equivalent is ‘… he saw in a dream.’

senses.def: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
to make known only the superficial and not the real character of something
senses.comment: In order to do justice to φαίνομαι in Matthew 23:28, it may be necessary in some languages to translate as follows: ‘on the outside you appear to people to be good, but you really are not’ or ‘… you only appear to people to be good’ or ‘… you make people think you are good, but you are not.’

senses.def: receiving and showing hospitality to a stranger, that is, someone who is not regarded as a member of the extended family or a close friend
glosses: receiving a stranger as a guest
senses.comment: To receive a stranger as a guest is sometimes expressed idiomatically as ‘to let a stranger sit at one’s table,’ ‘to offer a bed to a stranger,’ or ‘to let a stranger enter one’s house.’
